Cross-fitted text classifier baseline

Source: R/core-bench-baseline.R
hr_baseline_classifier.Rd

A ridge-penalised logistic regression on tf-idf features, fitted fold by fold so that every prediction comes from a model that never saw the item. Its accuracy is the floor a model configuration has to beat: a classifier trained on the same labels costs no model calls.

Usage

hr_baseline_classifier(
  texts,
  labels,
  folds = 5,
  cluster = NULL,
  seed = 1,
  lambda = 1,
  min_df = 2,
  max_features = 5000
)

# S3 method for class 'hr_baseline_classifier'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

texts

Character vector, one text per item.

labels

The label of each item: a factor, character, logical or numeric vector with at least two distinct values and no NA.

folds

Number of folds, at least 2.

cluster

Optional cluster of each item; folds then keep clusters whole.

seed

Seed for the fold deal, run on a private random stream so the session's stream does not move.

lambda

Ridge penalty, a positive number.

min_df, max_features

Passed to the tf-idf fit of each fold.

x

An hr_baseline_classifier.

...

Not used.

Value

An hr_baseline_classifier, a list with:

  • predictions: one row per item with item (position), id (names(texts), or the position), fold, label, predicted and correct.

  • prob: the out-of-fold probability matrix, one column per label.

  • folds: one row per fold with fold, n_train, n_test and n_terms.

  • train_items: the training item positions of each fold.

  • accuracy: the hr_prop_ci() row for the out-of-fold accuracy.

  • classes, settings and note.

Details

Folds. Items are dealt to folds folds under seed. Without cluster, the deal is stratified by label. With cluster (a document id, a source), whole clusters are dealt, so items that share a cluster are never split between training and test; with fewer clusters than folds, there is one fold per cluster. For each fold, the vocabulary and idf weights are fitted on the training texts only (hr_tfidf() with min_df and max_features) and applied to the held-out texts, so no word statistics from a test text reach its model.

Model. For two labels, one logistic regression of the second level against the first. Its coefficients maximise sum_i log L_i - (lambda / 2) * sum_j beta_j^2, with the intercept not penalised, fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares (each step a weighted ridge solve on the working response; Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009, section 4.4) with step halving. lambda = 1 is the same penalty as scikit-learn's LogisticRegression default (C = 1). For more than two labels, one model per label against the rest, with the probabilities divided by their sum; a label missing from a training fold gets probability 0 there. The predicted label is the most probable one, the first in level order on a tie.

Accuracy. The share of items whose predicted label equals the given one, with a Wilson interval from hr_prop_ci(). The interval treats items as independent; with cluster, read it as too narrow when clusters are large, and use the out-of-fold predictions in a benchmark report for a clustered interval.

References

Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. and Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd edition. Springer.

le Cessie, S. and van Houwelingen, J. C. (1992). Ridge estimators in logistic regression. Applied Statistics 41(1), 191-201.

See also

Other baselines: hr_baseline_ranker(), hr_tfidf()

Examples

texts <- c(paste("trial randomised placebo", c("adults", "children", "elderly")),
           paste("survey interview opinion", c("adults", "children", "elderly")),
           paste("randomised placebo trial", c("women", "men")),
           paste("opinion survey interview", c("women", "men")))
labels <- rep(c("trial", "survey", "trial", "survey"), c(3, 3, 2, 2))
fit <- hr_baseline_classifier(texts, labels, folds = 2)
fit
#> <hr_baseline_classifier> ridge logistic, 2 labels, 2 folds
#>   accuracy: 1.000 [0.722, 1.000], 10 of 10 out of fold
#>   training size per fold: 5, 5
fit$predictions
#>    item id fold  label predicted correct
#> 1     1  1    2  trial     trial    TRUE
#> 2     2  2    1  trial     trial    TRUE
#> 3     3  3    1  trial     trial    TRUE
#> 4     4  4    1 survey    survey    TRUE
#> 5     5  5    1 survey    survey    TRUE
#> 6     6  6    1 survey    survey    TRUE
#> 7     7  7    2  trial     trial    TRUE
#> 8     8  8    2  trial     trial    TRUE
#> 9     9  9    2 survey    survey    TRUE
#> 10   10 10    2 survey    survey    TRUE
